Stroop: Journey into the Rhino Horn War: The Back Story

By: Diana Lucas | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Stroop: Journey into the Rhino Horn War: The Back Story
Stroop: an Afrikaans word meaning to strip bare .. and that is behind Susan Scott and Bonne Du Bod’s documentary Journey into the Rhino War, exposing the truth behind the scourge of rhino poaching.

Stroop is a multi award- winning South African documentary. A wild life crime thriller investigation into South Africa’s rhino poaching crisis.

The film trails two first-time film-makers - director, Susan Scott and journalist and presenter, Bonne de Bod who took four years out of their lives to uncover the criminal underworld behind rhino poaching and international trafficking at home and abroad.


Further information:
It all started in the Kruger Park in 2013…Bonne was doing an update for SABC’s 50/50 on rhino poaching and while doing a piece to camera - sitting between two dead and stinking carcasses - she had a flash that someone needs to be telling this story. They both knew that unless the film was independent it would never make the light of day. Broadcasters have too many restrictions…National Geographic would find it too bloody; SABC would not expose the corruption. They envisaged it would take six months to produce. How wrong they were, the film consumed four years of their lives, they had to sell their homes, their investments and move in with their mothers who promised to cook for them and do their laundry.

Tracking the story between Africa and Asia, Bonne and Susan embedded themselves on the front-lines of the rhino species genocide. They had unprecedented access to the rangers in South Africa’s national parks and rhino sanctuaries, moving directly into the firing line.

In China, with no permission to film they went undercover on a tourist visa… going against some of the most ruthless criminal networks, risking their lives to show how the horn is processed, packaged and sold in Asia. It was here Bonne says strangely she had her hardest interview, not confronting ruthless criminals but talking to an Asian healer about rhino horn. As Bonne says the problem starts with an ancient mindset that the properties of the rhino horn have powerful and mythical qualities which results in the massive demand.

Bonne and Susan knew that if this documentary was going to make any waves, to be accepted in South Africa it it needed to win international awards. The world premier of Stroop was at the San Francisco Green Film Festival in September 2018 where it won the Green Tenacity Award. The film’s winning streak continued with Stroop winning best documentary at the prestigious San Diego International Film Festival (which only shows 13 films). To date Stroop has won 22 awards and the phone has never stopped ringing with people wanting this documentary, sight unseen.

Their message is also to show South Africans have the talent to tell their own stories and make their own films. They were brave enough to do it.

Sunday, 22nd September is World Rhino Day and M-Net will broadcast STROOP: Journey into the Rhino War. Before the broadcast Carte Blanche’s back story on the making of the documentary will deliver further insight into Bonne and Susan’s journey.

They are both passionate that South Africans see the extent of the crisis and to this end they have shown their film free at schools and educational facilities, to staff at the Kruger Park and even in Hong Kong prime time on their National Broadcaster. The message is strong and connects different worlds: from 16 year old Mapela from Polokwane who told them how Chen the Vietnamese activist in the film has inspired her to live her own dreams; to activists in Hong Kong who are working now to change their sentencing laws in regard to rhino poaching; to an electrician from Kruger’s Letaba camp who came up to them after the screening saying “ This is everyone’s problem from Afrikaner to Shangaan we are all not taking it seriously enough”.

Reviews have called Stroop, “a first hand never before seen panorama of the global trade in rhino horn” and its images are strong, sometimes brutal. With two rhinos being killed every day in the Kruger Park, and one every 8 hours in South Africa, Bonne and Susan are passionate that people must be empowered to act to protect these prehistoric animals whose time is running out.

“We made this film so no one can say I didn’t know.’

Script:


V/O A South African documentary investigating the crisis in the illegal trade of Rhino Horn has attracted global attention. Link: Stroop – Journey into the Rhino Horn War, is a raw hard hitting but emotional expose of poaching and the global trade in rhino horn. And it all started in the midst of the ongoing slaughter.

V/O 2013 and two massacred rhinos in the Kruger Park Susan: We were doing a rhino story. It was actually the very first crime scene or carcass that I had ever seen. It was actually a double carcass….

V/O Director, Susan Scott and Presenter, Bonne du Bod were filming for 50/50. Bonne: Susan said to me sit in between these two carcass’s and tell the viewer what you are seeing, what you feeling, and it was in that moment I was just so overwhelmed by questions, how can humanity be so absolutely cruel. Susan: You can’t walk away from seeing something like that and not be moved by it, …and we had to get the bottom of why.. Bonne: We thought we have to show South Africa what is really happening on the ground and that’s where the idea for STROOP was born.

Link: Susan and Bonne were adamant about one thing this film had to be entirely independent with no restrictions whatsoever but in this cash strapped world that’s easier said than done. Susan: Anytime we met with people when we were trying to find grant money or sponsorship they always said you are going to stay away from anything controversial and we said no actually we are going to show the controversial stuff and we are going to show the unpleasant stuff because that is what is happening to our rhinos.

They are beings just like us that are having this happen to them. Bonne: So we had to initially fund it ourselves we ended up selling our homes we moved in with our mothers, we cashed in our investments and we quit our jobs. We anticipated it to be a six month project but we found ourselves very quickly immersed in a world far larger and more dangerous than we ever anticipated, finally emerging from this odyssey only four years later
Link: Some of the scenes in STROOP are difficult to watch but they are balanced with a very difficult look at this endangered animal and in particular the trauma suffered by the young calves Bonne: Those little orphan babies crying, standing next to their mothers body because they wont leave their mothers body. You have to step away from yourself your ego, and realise its not about how I feel in that moment its about them.

V/O A strong narrative in their documentary took place at, wildlife rehabilitator Karen Trendlers’ rhino orphanage, and it was this story that took on a life of it’s own. Susan: We always knew we wanted to film with her but she is quiet a tough nut to crack. She is about the animals first and film crews very much second so it took a long time for us to get permission to go in and film with her. animals first if there is a rescue you very much keep your camera hidden away no loud noises and she grew to trust us.

V/O So when three years into their filming, Karen’s rhino orphanage was attacked by a poaching gang who not only slaughtered, two of the baby rhinos but raped one of the volunteers, one of Karen’s first calls was to the STROOP team.
Susan: Of course as a director I wanted to say can we come in and film but at the same time, these are real people who have gone through this trauma these are animals they have cared for that have been brutally savagely poached so you find you get very close to that line of pushing do we go into that space of uncomfortableness saying oh we want to come in and get the shots and so we didn’t ask and she said I think you need to come and film this I think it’s important for the world to see the after math of what has happened.

V/O Taking the viewer to the heart of the rhino poaching crisis meant travelling to the place where rhino horn is revered, the Far East Derek: A big decision to go to the Far East and film under cover specially without a permit. Susan: You can read as many NGO reports about the region and what’s happening with rhino horn usage inside Asia but we had to go in there we had to see what was going on, we had to bring it back home. Bonne: In order for us to capture the illegal side of things we had to become illegal ourselves. So we slip into Laos as tourists and we made our way from there to Bangkok to Hanoi to Hong Kong. We would book into a hotel with a credit card but we wont stay their we would go to another hotel pay cash and stay there we would use different sim cards , different cell phones not to be detected.

Derek: When did you feel your life was really in danger? Bonne: There was one moment where I was really really scared. We were in one of these underground back rooms and we were sitting around a table with these gangsters, and they were trading right in front of us. And the one guy turned to us and said let’s go lets take it to the factory we can show you how we rework the raw rhino horns into beautiful ornaments Myself and Susan we were looking at each other and we didn’t even think twice we were ok lets go. And when we got into the car, and that was the moment when I was Oh my gosh what are you doing…because we were literally covered in under cover cameras, button hole cameras key cameras..Susan even taped a Go Pro to my body so I wouldn’t be able to ditch it if they decided to search us at this point at this factory if they were even taking us their.

DereK: When you are looking at rhino horn in some of these upmarket shops it really doesn’t signify the bloody background. Right. And when I interviewed a rhino horn user there,….
STROOP Up Sound re Bonne looking at Rhino horn saying this represents death where I come from. … our rhinos are being slaughtered for this thing, and she said to me there is absolutely no connection for her between this product, between this piece of rhino horn and the animal.

Susan: This is just a product it’s a thing that is going to make money for me. It’s a thing that’s going to make me have status amongst my peers or its going to help me with my health, cure my cancer there is just no connection with the animal.

V/O Social media was vital in the filming of STROOP, not only helping fund the documentary through crowd funding but facebook, through which they developed a community of supporters. Susan A lot people said to us no one is going to watch this film people are tired about hearing about rhinos, with social media the more we would post on our journey the more the public shared reacted had comments and we’d look at each other and say there cant be rhino fatigue because people were on the journey with us they’re responding they are commenting so I don’t believe there is such a thing as rhino fatigue and I think the film shows that.

Link: STROOP has brought world wide attention to the rhino crisis and garnered a record number of awards but it’s two recent nominations that have their heads spinning. Susan: Jackson Wild, is considered the Oscars of Nature film making I remember Bonne when we were editing and she said Gosh wouldn’t it be nice if we are considered for the impact award And I said to Bonne there is no way we will be ever consider for that those are huge overseas broadcasters and here we are, nominated for best impact and Bonne nominated for best presenter.

Susan: Bonne we get out of here alive.speaks Afrikaans as her first language and there is our very own Bonne du Bod nominated for best presenter but she is very tough I remember a couple of times behind camera thinking she is not going to ask this oh yes she is going to ask this question ok I hope Bonne: 4 years filming so many people told us well you need to Americanise it if you want to make a success of it you need to get an American actor or voice over. And we just decided No this is a South African story made by two South Africans. Derek: Do you think STROOP has already changed minds? Bonne: Absolutely it’s been translated in four languages, in 77 countries, Derek: Even in Hong Kong? Even in Hong Kong, a couple of months ago it was shown on the national broadcaster during prime time in Cantonese which is phenomenal.. but we made this film for South Africans it is after all our heritage we are still losing 2 rhinos a day in the Kruger National Park. One every eight hours in the country, so we need South Africans to watch this film, to really see what is happening on the ground.

With two rhinos being killed every day in the Kruger Park, and one every 8 hours in South Africa, Bonne and Susan are passionate that people must be empowered to act to protect these prehistoric animals whose time is running out. “We made this film so no one can say I didn’t know.’
